title: 2 Kings 24:8–17
context: Jehoiachin reigns three months and does evil, and Nebuchadnezzar besieges Jerusalem; the king surrenders with his household and is taken to Babylon with the temple and palace treasures, as the LORD had said (cf. 20:17). The leaders, warriors, and craftsmen are deported, and Nebuchadnezzar makes Mattaniah king, renaming him Zedekiah. Both traditions read this as shared ground on judgment already announced, and Jehoiachin’s age is eighteen here and eight in 2 Chronicles 36:9. The deportation figures in 24:14 and 24:16 also differ from one another; these are noted without resolution.

verses.text: Jehoiachin was eighteen years old when he began to reign, and he reigned in Jerusalem three months. His mother’s name was Nehushta the daughter of Elnathan of Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Jehoiachin was eighteen years old when he began to reign, and he reigned in Jerusalem three months.” Arminian readers note the brevity of his reign.

2 Chronicles 36:9 gives his age as eight years and his reign as three months and ten days; the difference is a textual issue.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise note the difference in age between Kings and Chronicles, and leave it unresolved.

Both traditions treat the short reign as shared ground: the end of Judah’s independence is now near.

verses.text: He did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight, according to all that his father had done.
verses.arminianNotes:
“He did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight, according to all that his father had done.” Arminian readers note that Jehoiachin is held responsible for his own conduct.

The evaluation is brief, as in the notices of other late kings.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the continuing pattern of unfaithfulness among Judah’s last kings.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: each king is judged by the same standard of faithfulness to the LORD.

verses.text: At that time the servants of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up to Jerusalem, and the city was besieged.
verses.arminianNotes:
“At that time the servants of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up to Jerusalem, and the city was besieged.” Arminian readers note the swift arrival of the siege.

The narrator reports it plainly, without dwelling on its hardships.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the siege as the beginning of the judgment the prophets had foretold.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the threat that had been announced for years now reaches the city.

verses.text: Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came to the city while his servants were besieging it,
verses.arminianNotes:
“Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came to the city while his servants were besieging it.” Arminian readers note the personal presence of the Babylonian king.

The siege is not left to subordinates alone.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also note Nebuchadnezzar’s role, which Jeremiah describes in terms of serving the LORD’s purpose (cf. Jer 25:9).

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: an earthly king acts, yet the narrative places his actions under the LORD’s word.

verses.text: and Jehoiachin the king of Judah went out to the king of Babylon—he, his mother, his servants, his princes, and his officers; and the king of Babylon captured him in the eighth year of his reign.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoiachin goes out to the king of Babylon with his mother, servants, princes, and officers, and is captured “in the eighth year of his reign,” that is, Nebuchadnezzar’s. Arminian readers note that surrender may have spared the city for a time.

Jeremiah 52:28 dates a deportation to the seventh year; the dating is discussed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the king’s surrender as part of the unfolding judgment.

Both traditions treat the dating difference as an open issue, and they agree the verse reports the humbling of Judah’s king.

verses.text: He carried out from there all the treasures of the LORD’s house and the treasures of the king’s house, and cut in pieces all the vessels of gold which Solomon king of Israel had made in the LORD’s temple, as the LORD had said.
verses.arminianNotes:
Nebuchadnezzar carries away the treasures of the LORD’s house and the king’s house and cuts in pieces the gold vessels Solomon had made, “as the LORD had said.” Arminian readers note the fulfillment of Isaiah’s word to Hezekiah (20:17).

The loss of the treasures is reported soberly.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the precision of God’s word, spoken generations earlier.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the temple’s treasures could not protect a people who had turned from the LORD of the temple.

verses.text: He carried away all Jerusalem, and all the princes, and all the mighty men of valor, even ten thousand captives, and all the craftsmen and the smiths. No one remained except the poorest people of the land.
verses.arminianNotes:
“He carried away all Jerusalem, and all the princes, and all the mighty men of valor, even ten thousand captives, and all the craftsmen and the smiths. No one remained except the poorest people of the land.” Arminian readers note the loss of the city’s leadership.

24:16 gives different figures, and how the two counts relate is discussed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see a deportation that removes the leaders and skilled workers, leaving the poorest behind.

Both traditions treat the difference between 24:14 and 24:16, and the figures in Jeremiah 52:28–30, as textual issues left unresolved here.

verses.text: He carried away Jehoiachin to Babylon, with the king’s mother, the king’s wives, his officers, and the chief men of the land. He carried them into captivity from Jerusalem to Babylon.
verses.arminianNotes:
“He carried away Jehoiachin to Babylon, with the king’s mother, the king’s wives, his officers, and the chief men of the land.” Arminian readers note the fulfillment of warnings about the royal house (cf. 20:18).

The king who reigned three months now goes into exile.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the Davidic king himself carried into captivity, a heavy blow to Judah’s hopes.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground, and both note that the book returns to Jehoiachin at its close (25:27–30).

verses.text: All the men of might, even seven thousand, and the craftsmen and the smiths one thousand, all of them strong and fit for war, even them the king of Babylon brought captive to Babylon.
verses.arminianNotes:
“All the men of might, even seven thousand, and the craftsmen and the smiths one thousand.” Arminian readers note that these figures differ from the “ten thousand captives” in 24:14.

The relationship between the two counts is discussed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise note the different figures and leave them unresolved.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: Babylon took the warriors and craftsmen who could resist or rebuild, weakening Judah further.

verses.text: The king of Babylon made Mattaniah, Jehoiachin’s father’s brother, king in his place, and changed his name to Zedekiah.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The king of Babylon made Mattaniah, Jehoiachin’s father’s brother, king in his place, and changed his name to Zedekiah.” Arminian readers note that the renaming shows Babylon’s control over Judah’s throne (cf. 23:34).

Zedekiah reigns as a vassal king.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see Judah’s king now appointed by a foreign power.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: 2 Chronicles 36:10 calls Zedekiah Jehoiachin’s brother, a difference in relationship noted without resolution.
